interactions.title: Opening song: the Fraternity’s bargain with Agata
lines: DM: While this story has many beginnings, most who tell this tale start in the year of joyful rains long ago, when the Fraternity of the Empty Moon, a cult of werewolves, tried and failed to draw Pandemonium closer to Taelgar. They were defeated by the Dunmari outside Tokra, driven east and forgotten. Few sing the tale of the fraternity wandering in the wild lands in full, for even among the halflings not all parts of the song are known.

DM: But all sing of the moment a nameless werewolf, charismatic and smart, came to the ruined city of Kharsan, seeking to rally the offspring of Jinnik to his cause: to rebuild the fraternity and succeed, where his forebears had failed. Carrying the lore and prophecies of his ancestors rescued from the fall of the fraternity before and with a plan to return to that place near Tokra where Pandemonium lurks tantalizingly close, he gathered a small following and set them searching.

DM: He was looking for magic, for some item of power and significance that would attract the attention of another power in the desert: the hag Agata Dustmother. Here the storytellers sing the sour harmonies of Agata into the tale, the old, the old ally of Cha'mutte, left defeated on the edge of Dunmar, working in ways, large and small, to make life miserable for the Dunmari, the bitter notes of her melody echoing into the past and future. Strong in her own right, yes, but mostly using her large and growing collection of items of magical power to assert influence on.

DM: And then the key discordant note that will bring the tale back to the unlikely companions in—the chance that brought a great artifact of power from the Drankorian Empire—a scepter that gives its bearer the power of command—to the nameless werewolf leader and his subsequent meeting with Agata.

DM: The song of the Scepter of Command weaves through many ages far back before the Great War. And that story is one that is not told here today or this year, at least not in full, but it was found by werewolves, perhaps not entirely by chance.

DM: For this, Agata would trade much, the song tells. She would give the werewolves the way to break the mystical protections of Dunmar to let them enter unharmed and a distraction—a way that was something that would let them slip into Tokra unnoticed. And so the trade was made: the werewolf leader gifted a scroll to bring a demon of the Abyss to Karawa who could create an army of savage gnolls to unleash brutality and drive the Dunmari west, and a promise that Agata would deal with Shakun's defenses personally.

DM: They do not know it yet, but their stories are already beginning to be woven into the song of this year by halfling lorekeepers.

DM: Years later, halfling storytellers will recount how in a small village on the edge of Dunmar, four unlikely wanderers met, drawn together by chance and circumstance as dangers not seen for a generation began creeping across the border: wild creatures, full of all-consuming hunger, driven by the evil energy of the Abyss.
DM: The storytellers will weave the song of years past into the tale, for the song of this year, like all years, does not stand alone.
after: DM: It is here that the story returns to our travelers and Karawa, facing news of gnoll attacks and rumors of a demon cursed ruin in the north. Storytellers sing of their deeds, facing off against the demon and driving it back to the Abyss, freeing the hundreds of beasts kept in pens there for transformation into gnolls, the beast now safe to roam again on the Northern plains.

DM: Songs grow in the telling, and here many wonder, for Agata did nothing straightforward. Perhaps she too needed the werewolf leader, for she had made a promise not to cross north of the old trade road and in the deserts of the South, far too few animals live to create an army of gnolls. Some wonder whether she might have—what she might have done with an army had the four travelers not killed the demon. For the story tells that her servants waited in the demon-cursed fort, watching perhaps redirecting some of the hordes for her own purpose. It has long been known that she greatly desired the rumored dream magic of the Mystai of Bhishma, for example.

DM: Back to here, as with the gnoll threat contained, our story turns to Shakun and her servant Cintra. Here that tale is muddled in the song. Strange, for foreign gods keep secrets, even from the halflings.

DM: Yet if our heroes were listening, they would know the details, how Agata lured Cintra out of Karawa with dreams of her daughter's illness; deceived her into removing from Karawa the Heart of Shakun, the artifact that kept the divine protections on the eastern border of Dunmar intact. How Agata kidnapped Cintra's daughter Jumi and kept Cintra prisoner on threat of death of her daughter, and how they learned of all this, later than perhaps they would have liked, from Candrosa, Speaker of Shakun, skilled in many things, except making decisions in a crisis.

DM: Storytellers, though the details are murky, do not neglect our heroes at the moment they confront Agata in the desert south of Karawa. The tempo of the song rises, for here comes the halfling's moment of glory: the killing arrow from point blank range.
